newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians set to back Iliescu but dump his party.
newsitem.headline: Romanians set to back Iliescu but dump his party.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu holds a slender lead going into Sunday's Romanian general election, but his scandal-ridden party could lose, leaving him to face a parliament led by rivals seeking faster reform.
With a campaigning ban in force from Friday, Bucharest's tree-lined boulevards were again busy with shoppers after being thronged for two days with competing rallies.

Iliescu, in power since the fall of communism in 1989, heads most opinion polls with just over 30 percent, about four ahead of his nearest rival, academic Emil Constantinescu. A run-off round later this month is virtually certain.

But voters weary of widespread poverty and corruption appear ready to take control of the government away from Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), which lies second in polls for parliamentary elections also being held on Sunday.

In a long and often dreary television debate on Thursday featuring all 16 presidential hopefuls, Iliescu urged voters to stick with his moderate approach to reform and ignore rivals who denounce him as a vestige of the Communist era.
"We have stopped the decline of the economy and created the conditions for renewal and a better life," he told viewers.
"Those who say nothing has changed ought to look around. We cannot start from scratch every day. We cannot allow what our government has built to be destroyed by a new government."
Opposition parties have focused on plunging living standards and say Romania has fallen far behind Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic because of Iliescu's half-hearted embrace of reforms.
They also accuse Iliescu's PDSR of trying to engineer mass electoral fraud and rule out forming a coalition with it in the tortuous negotiations certain to follow Sunday's vote.
"We have a huge responsibility to the people and history," Constantinescu told 20,000 supporters of his Democratic Convention (CDR) on Thursday, ruling out a deal with the PDSR.
"There can be no backstage negotiations. There can be compromise. No one will forgive us if we squander this chance."
Iliescu won two previous elections handily in 1990 and 1992 and says he is happy to work within a French-style "cohabitation" arrangement with any party willing to cooperate.
His PDSR has been aligned with a variety of smaller parties during seven years in power, including nationalist groupings.
The opposition, led by the CDR and ex-Prime Minister Petre Roman's Social Democrats (USD), have formed a tactical alliance to try to ensure Sunday's vote is free of cheating.

Opposition groups say the PDSR has unfair control of the state media, has tried to manipulate distribution of "electors' cards," now abandoned in favour of identity cards, and has brazenly appointed its supporters to run polling stations.

The CDR has drawn up a "contract" with voters for faster reforms, and has pledged to resign if it is not implemented within a strict time frame. Roman seeks tax cuts, faster privatisation and help for the needy.
But the USD and CDR have adopted no clear strategy on forming post-election alliances and have spent much of the campaign sniping at each other.
